title: Phillip Island removed foxes; little penguin colony grew from 12,000 to 40,000
content:
Phillip Island’s little penguins once faced a crisis that threatened to erase much of their presence from the island. By the 1980s, nine of its 10 penguin colonies had disappeared, while the final colony on the Summerland Peninsula was also under pressure from introduced predators, habitat loss and human activity. According to Phillip Island Nature Parks, a long-running conservation effort combining fox control, habitat restoration, scientific research and land rehabilitation helped reverse that decline. The surviving little-penguin population grew from about 12,000 in the mid-1980s to an estimated 40,000 today. The story, detailed in the organisation’s pest-control, research and history records, shows how protecting wildlife often requires more than removing a single threat—it demands sustained cooperation between scientists, governments, local communities and visitors. Read on to know more:
A predator that changed the island
Phillip Island, also known as Milawul, is famous for the nightly arrival of little penguins at the Penguin Parade. Yet the sight that attracts visitors today was once at risk of disappearing.
Red foxes were introduced to Phillip Island in the early 1900s. Over time, they became one of the most serious threats to the island’s wildlife. Little penguins are especially vulnerable because they spend much of their lives at sea but return to land to breed, moult and raise their chicks. Their nests are often located in burrows or sheltered areas close to the coast, where they can be exposed to predators.
Phillip Island Nature Parks describes foxes as the little penguins’ biggest threat on land. By the 1980s, nine of the island’s 10 penguin colonies had become extinct. The remaining colony on the Summerland Peninsula, which includes the Penguin Parade, was also under threat.
The decline was not caused by foxes alone. Research identified several other pressures, including habitat destruction, housing development, traffic near penguin colonies, fire and domestic pets. Together, these threats made it increasingly difficult for penguins to survive and breed successfully.
Warning signs from research
The island’s conservation response was shaped by research. Population studies conducted during the 1980s showed that the last remaining penguin colony could disappear by the late 1990s if existing threats continued.
That warning encouraged authorities and conservation groups to take action. The Penguin Protection Plan, announced in 1985, included scientific research, habitat management, a fox-control program and the gradual buyback of houses in the Summerland Estate.
The housing estate had been built within the penguins’ habitat. As houses, roads and associated infrastructure were removed, the land could be returned to a more natural condition. This was a major undertaking and required years of planning, funding and rehabilitation.
Phillip Island Nature Parks says the buyback and removal of the Summerland Estate continued for decades, as per reports. The final houses and infrastructure were removed in 2010, after which an ongoing rehabilitation program was established to help penguins and other wildlife thrive.
This approach recognised an important conservation principle: removing a predator is not enough if the habitat remains unsafe. Wildlife needs places to shelter, feed, breed and raise young without constant disturbance.
The campaign against foxes
Fox control began as a coordinated effort involving farmers, rangers and conservation workers. According to Phillip Island Nature Parks, more than 1,000 foxes were removed over a period of 20 years.
The organisation initiated a dedicated Fox Eradication Project in 2006. Rather than relying on one method, the project used an integrated approach involving different techniques to locate and remove foxes across the island.
The goal was ambitious. Instead of simply reducing fox numbers, conservation teams aimed to remove foxes from Phillip Island altogether. This was important because even a small number of predators could threaten vulnerable colonies and prevent other species from recovering.
The campaign required persistent monitoring. Rangers and other workers had to search for signs of foxes, respond to sightings and prevent the animals from re-establishing a population. The work also formed part of wider pest management on the island, including programs targeting feral and roaming cats and rabbits.
In 2017, Phillip Island was declared fox-free after an intensive 20-year eradication program. The campaign was supported by the Victorian Government, Penguin Parade visitors, the Penguin Foundation and the Helen Macpherson Smith Trust.
Habitat restoration made a difference
The recovery of the little penguins was closely connected to the restoration of their habitat.
The Summerland Peninsula had once been transformed by housing development and human activity. Removing the houses allowed conservation teams to rebuild a landscape better suited to wildlife. The rehabilitation work helped restore vegetation, reduce disturbance and create safer areas for nesting.
The return of natural habitat also benefited species beyond little penguins. Short-tailed shearwaters and other coastal birds use the island’s protected areas, while the fox-free environment later supported the reintroduction of eastern barred bandicoots.
In 2017, the same year Phillip Island was declared fox-free, researchers released eastern barred bandicoots onto the Summerland Peninsula. The area had been rehabilitated from a former housing estate into a natural environment that supported a thriving little-penguin colony and migratory short-tailed shearwaters.
This illustrates how conservation gains can extend across an ecosystem. Protecting one habitat can create opportunities for several threatened species, especially when predators are controlled and human disturbance is reduced.
From 12,000 to 40,000 penguins
Phillip Island Nature Parks reports that extensive conservation work helped increase the number of little penguins from approximately 12,000 in the mid-1980s to an estimated 40,000 today.
The figures represent more than a simple population increase. They reflect the combined effect of predator control, habitat restoration, reduced development pressure, scientific monitoring and community involvement.
The Penguin Parade also provides a useful way to monitor changes. Guides count the number of penguins crossing the beach each night, and annual averages can offer insight into population trends. These counts do not represent every penguin on the island, but they help researchers track changes in the colony over time.
Conservation teams also monitor breeding success by studying the number of chicks fledged per breeding pair at selected sites. This helps researchers understand not only how many penguins return to land, but also whether they are successfully reproducing.
Such long-term monitoring is essential because wildlife populations can change in response to food availability, disease, weather, marine conditions, human activity and other factors. Regular data collection allows managers to identify problems early and adjust conservation strategies.
Research continues on land and sea
Although the fox eradication campaign was a major achievement, the work of protecting little penguins has not ended.
Phillip Island Nature Parks says its researchers study penguins in both terrestrial and marine environments. This is necessary because little penguins spend around 80 per cent of their time at sea, even though they depend on land for breeding.
Researchers use GPS trackers and other devices to study where penguins travel for food. Tracking has shown that many penguins feed within 50 kilometres of the island’s colony, while some individuals travel farther during winter, including towards Portland in Victoria and Port Phillip Bay near Melbourne.
Understanding these movements helps scientists identify potential threats in the marine environment. Changes in ocean temperature, prey availability, pollution and human activity can all affect the penguins’ ability to find food.
Research projects also examine feeding hotspots by combining information about where penguins go, how much they eat and what prey they consume. This evidence can help guide future conservation decisions as marine ecosystems respond to environmental change.
A model for community-led conservation
Phillip Island’s recovery story shows that successful conservation rarely happens through one dramatic action. It is usually built through many years of practical work.
The fox eradication program required rangers, farmers, scientists, government agencies, conservation organisations and local residents to work towards the same goal. Visitors also contributed through tourism, with Phillip Island Nature Parks stating that visits help fund research and wildlife conservation.
The island’s history also highlights the importance of acknowledging the Bunurong people, the Traditional Owners of Milawul. Phillip Island Nature Parks recognises the continuing connection of the Bunurong to the landscape and describes its role in healing Country and supporting Traditional Owner involvement in decisions about Country.
The little penguins’ recovery is therefore not only a story about numbers. It is a story about restoring a damaged landscape, learning from scientific evidence and changing the way people share space with wildlife.
What the future depends on
The increase from 12,000 to 40,000 little penguins is encouraging, but it does not mean the species is permanently secure on Phillip Island. Conservation gains must be maintained.
Foxes must remain absent. Other introduced predators, including feral and roaming cats, require continued management. Roads, pets, fires, rubbish, human disturbance and habitat damage can still affect wildlife.
The penguins’ time at sea also creates challenges that cannot be solved entirely on land. Their food supply may be influenced by changing ocean conditions, climate change and human activity. That is why Phillip Island’s conservation program combines population counts, breeding studies, tracking and marine research.
The lesson from Phillip Island is clear: wildlife recovery becomes possible when threats are identified early and addressed consistently. A colony that once appeared destined to vanish has grown substantially because people chose to protect its habitat, remove its predators and continue monitoring its future.
For the little penguins returning to shore each evening, that long-term commitment has made the difference between disappearance and survival.

title: El pueblito del Perú que hará historia durante la visita del Papa León XIV
content:
La expectativa en el norte peruano ha alcanzado un nivel histórico. El distrito de Zaña, ubicado en la región Lambayeque, se prepara para convertirse en el epicentro de un acontecimiento sin precedentes. Por primera vez en la historia de las visitas pontificias al país, un Santo Padre detendrá su recorrido en una localidad rural para reencontrarse con la comunidad que acompañó de cerca sus años de servicio pastoral.
El anuncio de la llegada del papa León XIV ha conmovido a los habitantes de este emblemático distrito, quienes recuerdan con afecto y gratitud la época en que Robert Francis Prevost ejercía su labor obispal en la diócesis de Chiclayo. Entre preparativos litúrgicos y una profunda devoción popular, Zaña aguarda la llegada del vicario de Cristo con el orgullo de saber que su nombre quedará grabado en los anales de la Iglesia Católica.
Zaña: de diócesis histórica a destino pontificio
Zaña no es una tierra ajena a la historia religiosa del Perú. Fundada en la época colonial y bendecida por el paso de figuras ilustres como Santo Toribio de Mogrovejo, la localidad suma ahora un hito contemporáneo de escala internacional. La conexión de León XIV con esta tierra se consolidó durante su periodo como obispo de Chiclayo, etapa en la que caminó por sus calles, celebró la eucaristía en sus templos y conoció de primera mano las necesidades de sus familias.
Para el padre David Farfán, párroco del templo Santo Toribio de Mogrovejo, esta visita trasciende lo protocolar. Durante su participación en un documental del Arzobispado de Lima, el sacerdote destacó la singularidad de la elección papal: “Es la primerísima vez que un Santo Padre incluye dentro de las grandes metrópolis a un pueblito”. Este gesto visibiliza a las comunidades periféricas y descentraliza la agenda habitual de los viajes papales, enfocando la atención de la fe católica en los rincones más sencillos del país.
Los recuerdos y testimonios de la comunidad zañera
El impacto de la visita se vive con especial intensidad en las calles y hogares de Zaña. Los vecinos recuerdan las misas dominicales, las visitas pastorales a los caseríos más alejados y el compromiso social desplegado por Robert Francis Prevost antes de su elección como sumo pontífice. Durante su gestión pastoral, el hoy papa León XIV impulsó diversas iniciativas de apoyo humanitario y fortalecimiento comunitario, especialmente en momentos de adversidad climática y económica en la región norteña.
Los testimonios locales coinciden en calificar su trato como cercano, sencillo y acogedor. Para muchas familias, volver a ver al obispo que caminó a su lado, ahora vistiendo el blanco pontificio, representa una bendición y un motivo de profunda gratitud. Las agrupaciones parroquiales y los fieles organizan comités de bienvenida para recibir al pontífice con cantos, testimonios y expresiones culturales propias de la identidad afroperuana y criolla de la zona.
Fechas y detalles del itinerario de León XIV en el Perú
La visita oficial del papa León XIV al Perú está programada del 11 al 16 de noviembre. Durante esta jornada de seis días, el Santo Padre cumplirá un itinerario que combinara los encuentros multitudinarios en las principales urbes del país con paradas de profundo valor afectivo y espiritual, como la programada en la Región Lambayeque.
La llegada del pontífice al distrito de Zaña se perfila como uno de los momentos más conmovedores de su viaje pastoral. Se espera que durante su estancia comparta un mensaje de esperanza y fraternidad con los comuneros, agricultores y familias que marcaron su itinerario misionero en el norte del país. La logística local se coordina entre las autoridades regionales, la Policía Nacional y la Conferencia Episcopal Peruana para garantizar la seguridad de los miles de visitantes y peregrinos que se trasladarán hacia la zona.
Un mensaje de transformación y renovación fe
Más allá del fervor inicial y la cobertura mediática, la llegada de León XIV plantea un desafío para los habitantes de Lambayeque. Como señaló el padre David Farfán, el verdadero impacto de este acontecimiento dependerá de la recepción interior que la comunidad dé a la enseñanza del pontífice. La visita no solo busca dejar un recuerdo en la memoria colectiva, sino también impulsar una renovación espiritual y social orientada a la solidaridad, la justicia y la atención a los más vulnerables.
El pueblito de Zaña, con su riqueza histórica y sus ruinas coloniales, se alista para escribir uno de sus capítulos más memorables. Con la cuenta regresiva hacia el 11 de noviembre en marcha, la expectativa crece en cada rincón del distrito, donde la fe y la memoria de un pasado compartido se unen para dar la bienvenida al papa León XIV.

title: Building a Black Honors Community
content:
California State University, Sacramento
When Naomi Thrower was applying to college, she knew she wanted the historically Black college or university experience but hesitated to leave the community she had built in California, which does not have a traditional HBCU.
So she applied to HBCUs across the country, as well as to California State University, Sacramento, the state’s first Black-serving institution.
“Sacramento State is the only California school I applied to. The rest were all East Coast HBCUs,” Thrower said. “I do have family on the East Coast, but none I felt strongly connected with. So I would be leaving my family, my friends, the life I’ve built here, and that was a little nerve-racking.”
Now a fourth-year deaf studies major, Thrower has found a community in the university’s Black Honors College, a first-of-its-kind program that provides a culturally responsive curriculum and inclusive academic community for students focused on the Black experience.
“It really provided me with a strong social foundation,” said Thrower, who was part of the college's inaugural cohort in 2024. “I knew everybody in my cohort, so when I was in my classes, when we started for the first day, I was nervous, but I already saw familiar faces, and so the [Black Honors College] provided me with that community feel.”
A growing community: Originally announced in 2023, Sacramento State’s Black Honors College offers smaller, specialized general education classes and is open to students of all races and majors. It also provides dedicated mentorship, paid internships, residential living-learning options and scholarships. The model offers a window into what can happen when an honors college centers Black history, culture and experiences in its curriculum while emphasizing community and belonging.
The Black Honors College admits incoming first-year students each fall, while transfer students and continuing Sacramento State sophomores and juniors can apply each spring. Students must have a 3.5 GPA at the time of application and maintain a 3.0 GPA or higher to remain enrolled.
Boatamo Ati Mosupyoe, dean of students and chief academic officer at Sacramento State, said the college initially planned to admit only 50 students in fall 2024, but growing interest led it to admit 80. The fall 2025 class grew to 262 students; this year's class is 414 students, bringing the total enrollment to 914.
Mosupyoe attributes that growth in part to the environment the college has sought to create, one that emphasizes students’ strengths rather than approaching them from what she described as a deficit perspective.
“We are creating a welcoming environment to the students,” Mosupyoe said. “This program doesn’t look at the students as deficient, and we don’t subscribe to a deficit model. We look at the potential of what these students are going to do.”
Matthew Ward, vice president of strategic enrollment management and chief enrollment officer, said the Black Honors College has become part of a broader effort at the university to intentionally support Black students and celebrate Black culture.
“We have lots of students who think about HBCUs but have to consider traveling across the country to go to an institution where they’re going to find that Black joy, Black excellence, Black dignity,” Ward said. “From what I’ve seen, in terms of the broader growth … word travels fast. There is definitely among students and families and school districts and educational leaders a real focus on Sacramento because it’s doing something that’s against the grain.”
That sense of community appealed to Manuel Tellez, a transfer student who grew up in Sacramento’s Oak Park neighborhood. Entering Sacramento State as a first-generation student, Tellez said he knew he needed the guidance of a strong Black community to feel comfortable and push himself academically, which he found in the Black Honors College.
“The Black Honors College pushed me to the next level [and] held me to a higher standard,” Tellez said. “Ever since then, my GPA has climbed, and I’ve been comfortable with going to school.”
Leland O’Neal, assistant program coordinator for the Black Honors College, said another strength of the college is the range of students and experiences represented within its cohorts.
“The pace of expansion has surprised me a little bit, but in a grand way,” O’Neal said. “We have students in that cohort, like Manuel, who are transfer students, but we also have students coming in who are as old as 69 or students who are as young as 19. So I think you really get a diverse array of perspectives and experiences.”
Building a network: As the Black Honors College has grown, so have its student supports. The college now offers financial literacy workshops, access to an in-house licensed therapist and events that celebrate Black culture. Mosupyoe said the number of professors affiliated with the college has also grown from 20 when the college began to 30 today.
“We have a community of administrators, staff and professors who are helping us really make sure that we provide what we have promised to students,” Mosupyoe said.
For Thrower, that support has extended beyond the classroom. She now works as a student assistant for the college and in that capacity has helped organize programming with the nonprofit Black Deaf Project to connect and socialize with students. The experience ultimately led her to an internship with the organization.
“The first piece of advice I got before college was that your net worth is your network,” Thrower said. “The Black Honors College has been that foundational network hub. I know people all over campus, and if I don’t know where to find some information, I know that I can go to the Black Honors College and they can direct me towards somebody who can help.”
(Updated 9/23, 12:20 p.m. to reflect the total number of students in the college.)
